meaningMnemonic: See the rock in the catapult ? It even has little legs to hold it steady so it can catapult better.
This looks like a claw of some kind already, making it quite easy!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means member .
See the guy? See how he was CUT IN HALF??? That must have been one heckuva slice to do that to a person.

There's a shellfish, but it's got some kind of fancy headgear. Is that… a crown, perhaps? It looks really valuable — and the shellfish wearing it must be even more valuable to be worthy of such a status symbol! Alternatively, you can remember this radical with its components: in the middle of the ground, there's a shellfish. Why? 'Cause it's super valuable. The safest place to keep a valuable shellfish is buried in the middle of the ground.
The beans radical and the beans kanji are exactly the same! Hints *toots*
readingMnemonic: These beans are from とう きょう . Everybody knows とうきょう has the best beans. What?! You didn’t know that? Tokyo’s beans are the best beans! Hints Imagine eating these beans from とうきょう . They’re the best beans you’ve ever had. Even if you don’t like beans, you love とうきょう beans. Mmm… beans, beans, とうきょう beans.

meaningMnemonic: A tree branch is exactly what it sounds like: the branch of a tree. Hints Picture a tree branch in your hands. Feel it. Smell it. It smells and feels like a tree.
readingMnemonic: You're smelling and feeling the branch when, suddenly, it starts screaming at you: " Eh, da d?" ( えだ ). The branch won't leave you alone. It follows you around screaming "Eh, dad?", thinking you're its long-lost tree branch father. Poor thing. Hints Picture the branch suddenly crying out, "Eh, Dad?" in a squeaky voice. You'd better find its real dad, otherwise this branch is never going to leave you alone.

meaningMnemonic: Take your fingers , step onto the forehead of your car , and brandish them in the air. Wave them around for everyone to see. Hints Imagine standing on top of your car, brandishing your fingers in the air while all of the cars stuck behind you honk angrily.
readingMnemonic: What are you brandish ing in your fingers? Your car's key ( き )! You want every driver and every car to know that you aren't going to be driving ever again! Hints You brandish the key in the air and then throw it into the woods. No more cars for you! Everyone should follow your example! Brandish your car keys in the air and throw them away!

meaningMnemonic: A slice with a knife is called a carve . Hints You carve meat, you carve wood, all with a slicing motion with a knife.
readingMnemonic: You work up a sweat trying to carve meat and wood all day, so you grab yourself a nice Coke ( こく ). You like Coke, and it goes well with meat and sawdust. Hints Imagine washing down all your hard carving work with an ice cold Coke.

meaningMnemonic: The claw radical and the claw kanji are exactly the same! Ravishing! Hints Lucky for you, this kanji has already etched its claw marks into your memory!
readingMnemonic: You sink your claw s into anything your two 目 ( つめ ) see, because you're such a fierce predator. If your two 目 can see it, your claws will get to it. Your claws are basically an extension of your two eyes, that's how skilled you are. Hints Imagine your claws darting out, almost automatically, as soon as your two 目 have seen your prey. Imagine catching your dinner that way.

meaningMnemonic: A child will ask if they want two water s because they need a grown-up's consent . Children aren't allowed to have whatever they want, they need to make sure it's okay and get consent first. Hints Picture the child finishing their first water. They look at a big stack of bottled waters, but they know better than to just take two more, they need consent first. "Excuse me, sir, could I please have two more waters?" the child asks.
readingMnemonic: "Of course my child, you have my consent ," comes the voice of the Shou gun ( しょう ). The Shougun is very pleased by this child, because he expects everyone to ask for consent around him. Hints You need to make sure to get express consent from the Shougun before you do most things. Especially if it's something like taking more than you've been given.

meaningMnemonic: Your mouth was slice d open by a terrible cough . Hints You've heard of a hacking cough, right? Well, this is worse. It's a slicing cough, and it's sliced right through your mouth, too. Imagine it flapping around while you cough.
readingMnemonic: Oddly enough, some people find your cough sexy ( せき ). Hints That slicing cough opened up a nice gravelly, sexy voice. Between coughs, you start noticing all the looks you're getting. You realize your cough is making you really sexy to all the people around you. Cough cough cough.

meaningMnemonic: In a greenhouse , a towel becomes a curtain as soon as you hang it. Greenhouses are made of windows, it's all glass, there are no walls. So when you put a towel in there it turns into a curtain. It has no choice but to cover a window, after all. Hints Imagine hanging towels over all the windows in the greenhouse. They're really fuzzy, thick curtains now.
readingMnemonic: You're hanging these towel curtain s because you need a quiet place to eat a Big Mac ( まく ). But you're a little ashamed. Big Macs aren't really good for you, but this stupid greenhouse has too many windows and everyone can see you stuff your face. So that's where the towel curtains come in. Hints Imagine hiding in a greenhouse blocked off with towel curtains, stuffing your face with Big Macs. No one can shame you in here. You can eat as many as you want. And hey, you can use the curtains as napkins too.

meaningMnemonic: You use thread in your construction project to hold everything together. The color of the thread is a deep red , and it gives everything a crimson look. Hints Because thread isn't that strong, you have to use A LOT (to hold things like beams in place). So, the deep red or crimson thread actually stands out a lot in this construction project.
readingMnemonic: You're done, and the whole building is a deep red crimson color (it takes a lot of thread to hold a whole building in place). It's time to show the client, Emperor こう いち , the finished product. Hints こういち walks up with a big smile on his face. "I love the color crimson!" he exclaims. "It's the same deep red color as my enemies." Hint: When you see 工 in a kanji it will often take the こう reading.

meaningMnemonic: An arrow is what this turkey lack s. For a turkey, that is a delight . Hints A turkey that lacks an arrow is a delighted turkey.
readingMnemonic: Delight is what Genghis Khan ( かん ) felt when he saw his turkey friend, sans an arrow. Hints He loves his turkey friend, and every time he sees it he squeals with delight.

meaningMnemonic: The woman sitting on that stool is actually a dude . Oh oops! You thought he was a woman because of his long hair and the way he was sitting. Maybe you shouldn't be judging people based on their looks! Hints Dude, I can't believe you called that dude a woman. What's wrong with you?!
readingMnemonic: You only found out this dude wasn't a woman when a do g ( ど ) ran up and the dude stood up. He started rubbing the dog's face saying, "Who's a good boy? Who's a good boy? Not you! Me! I'm the best boy of them all. Because I am a dude, the best of all boys! HAHAHAHA!" Hints Look at the poor dog. He's not a dude and now he doesn't think he's a good boy, all because of this other dude. Was he sitting on the stool this whole time, waiting to make this dog feel bad? I guess you'll never know...

meaningMnemonic: The ear and the mouth of a king are holy . The king has holy hearing and holy eating abilities. This king is divine. Hints See the holy ear and mouth of this king. They glisten and glitter and people write hymnals about their holy prowess. Imagine a song playing as you witness their holy majesty.
readingMnemonic: This holy king has heard of you and your special sa ber ( せい ) that glows with pure, blue light. Specifically, the holy king wants to use it on his food! Hints The holy king heard you turned into a prosperous plate and used the saber to cut your food and now he wants to try it too. As he holds your saber, a holy circle forms around it, making it sparkle and shimmer! Your saber is holy now too!!

meaningMnemonic: If the fingers on a turkey are pointing right at you, you can infer that it wants revenge. This turkey knows you killed his brother for dinner last night, and now it's going to make you pay. You infer that this turkey is going to take its fingers and wrap them around your neck. Hints Imagine a turkey is pointing at you with its fingers. The gears in your brain begin to slowly turn. From looking at the turkey to its fingers and back to the turkey, you can infer that something bad is probably about to happen to you.
readingMnemonic: You were able to infer the turkey's plan, so now it's your turn. You look around and see the only way out... is to swi ng ( すい ) to safety! How did I infer that, dear Watson? Why, isn't it obvious! There are vines here. Turkeys can't fly. So I shall swing my way to freedom! Hints Picture yourself as Sherlock Holmes, you inferred your way to freedom, swinging away on a conveniently-placed vine.

meaningMnemonic: Your moon storehouse is another storehouse you own. Remember how your regular storehouse holds zombies (from the kanji 蔵 ?). Your moon storehouse is on the moon, and it is filled with internal organs . Hints Your moon storehouse has internal organs because 1) you have to keep them far away from the zombies or they'll go berserk, and 2) you think it's funny to see them bounce around in low gravity. Boing, boing, boing, haha look at that internal organ.
readingMnemonic: Where did you get all these internal organ s from? You actually harvested them from the zo mbies ( ぞう ) from your other storehouse. Hints Basically, you store zombies in your regular storehouse, harvest their organs, then launch them into space where they are put into a storehouse on the moon where the zombies will never be able to find them again.

meaningMnemonic: Raise your fingers to another member and you'll receive a loss in return. You should never hurt a member of your team, group, or society. It's just wrong. And you'll incur a loss as punishment for your bad deeds. Hints Imagine raising your fingers to slap, hurt, or point angrily at a member of your own team. How dare you! I hope you're ready for some deep, personal loss.
readingMnemonic: Unfortunately for you, payment is in the form of the loss of your son ( そん ). The loss of any family member is horrible, but this was your son. He was your favorite child. You loved him. But that's the loss you must bear for raising your fingers to a team member. Hints Picture your son. Your future son, maybe even your animal son, if you don't want to have real kids. Now imagine the loss of that son. Nooooo!

meaningMnemonic: Seeing a stone and some horns on the ground next to a piece of poop and another piece of poop , you try and pick each of them up with a magnet . The magnet fails to pick up either piece of poop. The magnet doesn’t pick up the horns either. But wait! The magnet picks up the stone! Hints Imagine yourself trying to pick each object up off the ground with your magnet. Hear the clink of the stone against metal as the magnet lifts it off the ground. Must be some iron in it or something.
readingMnemonic: You’re pretty excited that you lifted something up with your magnet . Science is cool! But then you hear someone laughing behind you. It’s Je sus ( じ )! Jesus was using his magic to levitate the stone all along, it wasn’t your magnet. Darn it Jesus! You’ve fooled me for the last time! Hints Imagine Jesus snickering behind you as the stone falls to the ground once again. Imagine running after Jesus so you can catch him and give him a piece of your mind. He’s always playing tricks on you.

meaningMnemonic: They say accidentally firing a catapult is an unforgivable mistake . They say you shot the catapult at your own castle. Even though it was an accident, it’s still a mistake you will never be forgiven for. Hints Imagine shooting the catapult on your own people by mistake. Hear the catapult whoosh as your heart drops into your stomach. Oh, what a terrible mistake you’ve just made.
readingMnemonic: This mistake alerts Go dzilla ( ご ), who thinks it's town destroying time. He barrels over the hills, sees where you mistakenly catapulted your own people, and proceeds to stomp on the rest of it for you. Hints Picture Godzilla jumping happily on the castle and surrounding town you hit by mistake. This is probably the worst mistake you've ever made.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami was the original event to mark the origin of Japan. A big tsunami came and uncovered the islands of Japan. It's the origin of all life, as far as Japanese people are concerned. Hints Picture the original tsunami used in the origin story of Japan (never mind that we just made this up). It was huge. Bigger than anything you've ever seen. And without it you wouldn't have your precious anime and manga.
readingMnemonic: This tsunami was also the origin of Gen ji ( げん ), from "The Tale of Genji." Just think, without this origin, Japan wouldn't exist and neither would the first Japanese heartthrob, Genji! Hints The origin of Genji was the origin of all Japan: a big ol' tsunami.

meaningMnemonic: If it's made of thread , your barracks will be pure . If you build it out of clay or bricks or wood, it will inevitably have some dirt in it. Build it out of thread to keep it pure of... well, impurities. Hints Imagine a barracks made of pure thread. No brick or clay barracks can compete with yours, as long as you make it out of pure, unadulterated thread.
readingMnemonic: Unfortunately, this pure thread barracks can only be used in June ( じゅん ). Any other time of year there will be snow and rain and mud that will get tracked into the pure barracks and ruin them. But June is the cleanest, most pure month, so you can use it then. Hints Okay, so maybe building a pure barracks that you can only use in June was a bad idea, but it's there now and I don't want you getting it dirty, so just use it when I say so, okay?

meaningMnemonic: You want some flowers to put on the canopy above your helicopter to keep the bird s away, so you ask people what they would recommend . Hints You've bought flowers before, but you really don't know which ones would work best to stop birds from landing on the canopy and pooping on your helicopter.
readingMnemonic: You ask for a recommend ation from the cen taur ( せん ) that owns the local flower shop. Now he's walking around your helicopter canopy and staring at the birds, nodding. Hints I hope the centaur recommends a cheap flower... but with your luck flowers that keep birds away will cost a fortune.

meaningMnemonic: Into a well , a drop of rice falls from your rice bowl . You were eating out of your rice bowl on the side of a well, and some rice fell out of your rice bowl and this drop of rice proceeded to fall all the way down. Hints You lost a drop of rice from your rice bowl. Feel sorrow for the lost rice as you watch it fall down the well and hear it splat into the water below.
readingMnemonic: Just then, the don ( どん ) of your local mafia shows up, steals your rice bowl , and shoves you into the well. You’d gotten on the don’s bad side, so he came to teach you a lesson. The don steals your rice bowl and shoves you into the well. Hints Hear the don shout, “See ya, sucker!” as he pushes you into the well. You’ve just lost a drop of rice, now your rice bowl, and now you’re all wet in a well. Worst day ever.

meaningMnemonic: Set up your canopy , attach some meat to it, and the meat will eventually rot . Hints Imagine the smell of rotten meat hanging from your canopy. Now no one wants to come near here.
readingMnemonic: You let meat rot . You're a foo l ( ふ ). That's really all I can say at this point. Hints What, did you think attaching this meat to the canopy would make it turn into jerky or something? Fool...

meaningMnemonic: There's a tsunami coming, so you put your fins on, open your mouth wide, and try to run alongside it. Hints Your mouth is open so you can scream, because this is probably a bad idea.
readingMnemonic: You're able to run alongside the tsunami for about ten seconds before everything en ds ( えん ). Hints Okay, so maybe trying to run alongside a tsunami with just some fins and a mouth full of screams and terror wasn't the best idea. But at least everything ended while you did... uh... something unique?

meaningMnemonic: You need to take a body measurement before you can shoot . Whether it's for a photo shoot, you're gonna shoot them with a gun, or if you're about to shoot them full of radiation for X-rays, you need the right measurements of that body first. Hints Imagine someone measuring your body before they shoot you. You hope it's the good kind of shoot and that you're not going to die.
readingMnemonic: This shoot is being done by a sha man ( しゃ ). Not only is he doing the body measurements for the shoot, but he's also going to be shooting you with a shot so you don't get the flu. Hints Shamans are just a different kind of doctor. And this shot is going to save you from getting the flu, which could kill you. Make sure you always go to the local shaman and schedule a shooting.

meaningMnemonic: A magic thread fell from the roof onto the leader of a hundred people, causing him to shrink ! Hints Picture one hundred people under the same roof watching in horror as their leader suddenly shrinks to nothingness before them.
readingMnemonic: As the leader shrink s, the hundred people start screaming and running around the entire place. As a result, everything is shook ( しゅく ) up. Especially the poor, shrunken leader, who gets knocked around the most. Hints The leader gets shook so badly, he can't even call out to his people. They're going to trample his tiny, shrinking body!

meaningMnemonic: A samurai uses a jackhammer while a stick -wielding Wolverine sips water and supervises him. Clearly, he's Wolverine's slave , and he's being forced to do some kind of grueling manual labor unbefitting of his samurai rank. Hints If the samurai doesn't make progress in his jackhammering, Wolverine will hit him with the stick and withhold water from him. Sadly, this is what life is like for a slave.
readingMnemonic: You don't like seeing slave s. As you walk by, you hand the enslaved samurai a ray ( れい ) gun so he can free himself. Hints The samurai slave uses the ray gun to shoot Wolverine and run away, freeing himself from slavery. You watch as Wolverine writhes in pain on the ground, wounded by the ray gun. Serves him right for keeping slaves, I guess.

meaningMnemonic: There's some rice in the shape of a nine on a cross and this is stylish . The rice grains are arranged to form the number nine. This number nine is prominently displayed on the cross, and it's stylish to carry it around and be seen with it. Hints Imagine hefting this cross with the rice in the shape of a nine on it. You don't feel stylish, but society tells you that you are. You're stylish.
readingMnemonic: It's also stylish to swi ng ( すい ) the cross around while you wait for things. You're waiting at a bus stop so you swing the cross around violently. You swing it so violently that the rice comes flying off! Hints See the rice fly through the air from you swinging the cross. Hear it as it clatters to the ground. This cross just isn't as stylish anymore now.

meaningMnemonic: You are so sick that you've come to look like the humble stool : thin . Eerily thin, in fact. Hints Imagine standing behind a stool and being able to disappear behind it completely. That's how thin this sickness has made you.
readingMnemonic: When you're this thin , your sou l ( そう ) is visible from outside of your body too. Hints Picture your soul pulsing through your thin body. You have no body fat to cover it up, so everyone can see it pulsing and lurking in there. This is why you're hiding behind one of the humble stools in your house.

meaningMnemonic: If your mouth has dirt in it, you're going to throw up . That's just a fact. Hints Imagine how queasy you're feeling with all this dirt in your mouth. You're going to have to throw up now — you've passed the puke threshold.
readingMnemonic: When you throw up it sounds like you're shouting, " Hah ( は )!" Then all the dirt-puke comes out in a wave. It's less of a laugh "hah" and more of an oh no I'm throwing up "hah." Hints Imagine the sound you made the last time you threw up. It sounded like you were saying "hah!" from the bottom of your tummy.

meaningMnemonic: The valuable radical and the valuable kanji are the same! Hints The most valuable kanji are the ones you don't have to learn from scratch.
readingMnemonic: Most valuable things require a key ( き ) to be accessed. I mean, you've gotta keep your valuable stuff safe, right? Best to keep it under lock and key. Hints Just be careful not to lose track of the key. Otherwise, your valuable stuff is going to be safe from everyone… including you.

meaningMnemonic: When a thread loiter s on the horns of a coat rack , it's always vertical . By loitering I mean hanging around, and by horns I mean the little bits sticking off a coat rack that you hang your vertical threads on. Obviously. Hints Picture this thread hanging (loitering) on the horn of your coat rack. Imagine yourself putting it there, then observing how it hangs. Naturally it's going to be vertical, right? That's just physics, baby.
readingMnemonic: Whether or not a thread will hang vertical depends on how you 立て る ( たて ) your coat rack. If you 立てる the coat rack properly, the threads will hang off it in a perfectly vertical way. On the other hand, if you 立てる it carelessly, things might end up kind of kind of diagonal and weird. Hints Think about how careful you're going to be when you 立てる your coat rack to make sure the stuff hanging from it is as vertical as can be. If things aren't perfectly vertical, you'll dismantle it and 立てる it again till they are.

meaningMnemonic: Boot s give you the power to work ! That's why so many professions require you to have work boots. Hints Imagine putting your boots on and suddenly being filled with the power and energy to work hard and efficiently.
readingMnemonic: You need boots to give you the power to work for the Kin g ( きん ) of England. Really, all work is for the King, since everything is for him. But even he wears boots. And they give him the power to uh... king over things. Hints Picture yourself in work boots. Now picture the King in work boots. Yours are worn and beaten up and his are clean and look brand new. But at least you both have them, which means you both work at least a little!

meaningMnemonic: Take your fingers and dry them. Then dry them again. This is what you do when you are in worship . Once you go into your place of worship, and again before you leave. You have really sweaty fingers, and you can't worship anyone or anything if you have wet hands. So you dry them! Hints Picture your sweaty, sweaty fingers. Dry them off before you enter a place of worship! No god wants to deal with your weird, damp hands.
readingMnemonic: Once you're dry and in wherever your worship is, you begin with a hai ku ( はい ). Really all places of worship have their own version of the haiku, and heck, the 5-7-5 rule is just a guideline, so everyone is doing it pretty close to right anyway. Hints Imagine being in your place of worship. Close your eyes and say a haiku: So I won't offend Lord Crabigator-sama I dry my hands now.

meaningMnemonic: Something that is pure fur is pure fur... but what kind of fur? In this case it's wool, making this mean all wool .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

meaningMnemonic: You've got some deep red leaves . You'll usually see those during autumn, which makes this autumn leaves . Just red leaves is fine too, though. sentences.japanese: それがどんな汚い手を使ってでも勝たなきゃいけない試合だってことには賛成するよ。
sentences.english: I agree that it’s a game we must win by any means necessary.

meaningMnemonic: I must say humbly that I want to get into this position, so I'm planning to apply for it and to submit an application . 申し込む isn't just about applying, though. It's about officially communicating desires, whether you want to propose marriage, challenge someone to a game of tennis, or even offer a donation to a good cause.
readingMnemonic: The readings come from the word 申す and the kanji 込 , stuck together... humbly.

sentences.japanese: JLPTのテストに申し込むのを忘れてしまった。
sentences.english: I forgot to apply for the JLPT exam.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means wound , and this verb is intransitive, so it means to be damaged or to go bad . After all, fruit with a wound on it is going bad, isn't it?
readingMnemonic: This shares the same reading as 痛む . The meanings are similar too, so that should be easy to remember, unless your brain was damaged by these mnemonics or something.

sentences.japanese: このアボカド、昨日買ったところなのにもう傷んでるよ。
sentences.english: I bought this avocado yesterday and it’s already gone bad.

sentences.japanese: 日の光が当たる所に置いていたせいで、箱が傷んでしまったみたい。
sentences.english: It looks like the box was damaged because I put it in a place where it was exposed to sunlight.

sentences.japanese: 生クリームは傷みやすいから、使ったらすぐに冷蔵庫に閉まってね。
sentences.english: Fresh cream spoils easily, so please put it back in the fridge as soon as you finish using it.

meaningMnemonic: If 染める is "to dye," then this is to be dyed . You aren't doing the dyeing, because you know that if you did it you would have done things right, unlike the other person who dyed your hair. This person marr ed ( まる ) it up really bad.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 染める .

sentences.japanese: 子供たちがこの悪い環境に染まってしまうことを心配してるのよ。
sentences.english: I’m worried that our kids will be tainted by this bad environment.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji is work which means this verb has something to do with working. It's not straight up "to work," instead it's " to work for " or " to be employed at ."
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the other word that means "to work as" ( 務める ). Remember this and you'll be able to remember the reading for this word too.

sentences.japanese: 娘が小学校に上がったので、私は図書館に勤め始めました。
sentences.english: I started working at a library ever since my daughter got into primary school.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means carve so the verb version is to carve .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You don't have a knife for your steak, so you have to carve it using the key za g ( きざ ) technique. You take a key and zag it through the steak repeatedly until you're able to cut up some zaggy bite-sized pieces.

sentences.japanese: 葱を刻むのは面倒くさいよ。
sentences.english: I can't be bothered to cut up the green onion.

sentences.japanese: 効率が第一だということを、しっかり心に刻んで置いてください。
sentences.english: Efficiency is our top priority — be sure to keep that firmly in mind.

meaningMnemonic: You cause the departure of something in you (to the outside), then brandish it for all to see. You're sending it out to show everyone. That's why this means to exhibit or to demonstrate . 発揮する means to bring out one's abilities, strengths, or qualities in a visible or effective way. It's often used when someone performs well under pressure or maximizes their potential in a given situation.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The はつ becomes はっ , though.

sentences.japanese: 問題解決にリーダーシップを一番発揮していたのは誰ですか。
sentences.english: Who demonstrated the most leadership in solving the problem?

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. Huh — another verb for trickery ? Yup, but this one is for a specific kind of trickery: it means to falsely impersonate . 騙る refers to pretending to be something you're not, especially by claiming a false identity, status, or story. It's narrower than 騙す , because it specifically involves misrepresentation — like when a scammer tries to pose as someone they're not.
readingMnemonic: This word uses a different kun'yomi reading than the one you learned with the kanji and with 騙す . Here's a mnemonic to help you remember it: The punishment for trying to falsely impersonate someone is to get launched out of a cata pult ( かた ). If you want to pose as someone else and scam innocent people, you'd better prepare to get loaded into a catapult and jettisoned into oblivion. Alternatively, you can think about how this word is like the evil version of 語る (to talk). You're talking, but this time you're using your words to fraudulently claim to be someone you're not.

sentences.japanese: 人の名を騙る
sentences.english: to impersonate someone

sentences.japanese: 私の名前を騙る
sentences.english: to impersonate me

sentences.japanese: 予言者を騙る
sentences.english: to pose as a prophet

sentences.japanese: 息子を騙る
sentences.english: to claim to be someone's son

sentences.japanese: 有名人を騙るアカウントに注意してください。
sentences.english: Be careful of accounts impersonating celebrities.

sentences.japanese: 彼女は記者を騙って情報を集めた。
sentences.english: She pretended to be a reporter and gathered information.

sentences.japanese: 本人を騙る人物がSNSに現れた。
sentences.english: Someone falsely impersonating the individual surfaced on social media.

sentences.japanese: 市の職員を騙る電話がかかってきた。
sentences.english: I received a call from someone posing as a city employee.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means thin so the verb version is to get thin .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: If you want to get thin , just join the Ya nkees ( や ). They run their players around those four bases so much they all get thin quicker than you can throw a ball.

sentences.japanese: 「痩せたい」と、言い始めてから二年が経ちます。
sentences.english: It's been a couple years since I started saying, "I want to lose weight."

sentences.japanese: 私の村にいる野良犬のほとんどは痩せていますよ。
sentences.english: Most stray dogs in my village are skinny.

sentences.japanese: 会話が途切れて気まずくなった時は、とりあえず「最近、痩せた？」と言うことにしている。
sentences.english: When it gets silent and awkward during conversations, I make it a rule to just say, "Have you lost weight lately?"

meaningMnemonic: To do loss to something means you are doing something to make something have loss. This is to harm or to injure .
readingMnemonic: In order to harm your opponent, you go way overboard. You soak ( そこ ) them in acid. Soaked head to toe. Too far man, too far.

sentences.japanese: 働きすぎてあんたが健康を損なうんじゃないかって、心配してるのよ。
sentences.english: I’m worried that you may ruin your health by working too hard.

meaningMnemonic: You worship only the things you see . So, in order to see if something is worth worshiping, you'll go to have a look at that thing. And just so you know, this is a very formal word used when you're trying to be polite. So keep that in mind, please!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: あなたが描いた日陰に座っている少女の絵を拝見しました。
sentences.english: I took a look at your painting of a girl sitting in the shade.

meaningMnemonic: Giving consent to someone is similar to humbly listening to and accepting their words. So this word means to humbly hear and to accept . 承る is a humble version of 聞く . Its past form 承りました is commonly used in professional settings to respectfully acknowledge and accept requests, information, or tasks.
readingMnemonic: You received ( 受けた ) some information. Now, you are going to take that information that you received and then revolve it ( 回る ) around in your head to think about it. Hmmm... hmm... Ok, I like what I'm hearing. I am going to accept what you said. Thank you.

sentences.japanese: ご伝言を承りましょうか。
sentences.english: Would you like to leave a message?

meaningMnemonic: You つける (attach) a wound to someone or something. In other words, this means to hurt someone , or to scratch or to damage something.
readingMnemonic: The reading is 傷 . If you remember the reading for that you got this too.

sentences.japanese: コンタクトレンズを傷つけちゃったかも。
sentences.english: I might have scratched my contact lens.

sentences.japanese: 私たちも知らないうちに人を傷つけているかもしれません。
sentences.english: We may also be hurting people without knowing it.

sentences.japanese: 誰だよ？俺のベンツに鉄棒で傷つけやがったのは？！見つけたらただじゃおかねえぞ！
sentences.english: Who the heck damaged my Mercedes with an iron bar?! They'll pay for this!

meaningMnemonic: Departure and shoot something off. If you do that to something, you are going to launch it.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: ミサイルは予定通り発射された。
sentences.english: The missile was launched as planned.

sentences.japanese: ロケットは垂直に発射した。
sentences.english: The rocket took off vertically.

meaningMnemonic: 汚れる is "to get dirty." This is when you make something dirty, aka " to make dirty ." You know that this is the version where you make things dirty yourself because when you make someone dirty with all that poop you're flinging, they sue ( す ) you immediately. This happens a lot.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 汚れる , so if you know that you can read this. Note that the reading よごす is generally used for making things physically dirty, whereas けがす means making someone or something impure in a figurative way.

sentences.japanese: 手を汚す
sentences.english: to dirty one's hands

sentences.japanese: 水を汚す
sentences.english: to make the water dirty

sentences.japanese: 海を汚す
sentences.english: to pollute the sea

sentences.japanese: 綺麗なスタイが無くなっちゃった。うちの赤ちゃんが全部汚しちゃって。
sentences.english: We are out of clean bibs. Our baby boy got them all dirty.

sentences.japanese: アイツは自分では決して手を汚さない、ずるい男だ。
sentences.english: He is a cunning man who never dirties his hands.

sentences.japanese: ひどい！許せません。神聖な場所を汚された気分です。
sentences.english: Terrible!!! I cannot tolerate it. It feels like a sacred place has been defiled.

meaningMnemonic: 越す is "to go beyond." Now you're going beyond your home and pull ing everything with you to go to another home. You are trying to move / to move homes .
readingMnemonic: The readings come from 引く and 越す put together. Careful of that っ .

sentences.japanese: 「パパ、フグと私、結婚して日本に引っ越すつもりよ。」「俺の目の黒いうちはそんなことはさせないぞ。」
sentences.english: "Dad, Fugu and I are getting married and moving to Japan." "Not while I’m alive, you won’t."

meaningMnemonic: 越す means "to go beyond." 追 is follow . If you are following someone, and then you go beyond them, you have overtaken them. That's why this word means to overtake or to surpass .
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 追う and 越す put together into one. You can overtake this word now that you know that.

sentences.japanese: 他の自転車走者を追い越す時、いつも挨拶代わりに手を振ります。
sentences.english: I always wave my hand to say hi whenever I pass other bikers.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means throw up so the verb version is to throw up or to puke or to spit .
readingMnemonic: The reading is from the reading you learned with the kanji. HA HA HA! Barf.

sentences.japanese: 「遅れてごめんなさい。朝、少し気分が悪くて吐いてしまって。」「大丈夫だよ。遅れても来ないよりはましだよ。」
sentences.english: "I’m sorry I’m late. I was sick and threw up this morning." "It’s okay. Better late than never."

meaningMnemonic: You know the kanji 込 means into . This verb is transitive, meaning you are doing the action. If you “do something into something” you are putting it into that thing. So this means to put in or to load something .
readingMnemonic: Lucky for you, the reading you learned with the kanji is the one you use here. In case you need a hand with the okurigana, here’s a mnemonic for you: You always try to put in your emotions into the mail ( める ) you send. You don't just load your mail with words, but also with emotions, to make it truly heartfelt mail.

sentences.japanese: ショットガンに弾を込める時間がなかったんだ。
sentences.english: I didn’t have enough time to load rounds into the shotgun.

sentences.japanese: もっと気持ちを込めて演技しろよ！それでもプロの劇団員か？
sentences.english: Put more emotion in your performance! Are you really a professional theatrical actor?

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means recommend so the verb vocab version is to recommend . This word is often used in a positive context for recommending things, actions, and people by implying or pointing out their charms, merits, or both. Although 薦める and 勧める are similar, there are subtle differences between the two. 勧める is often used to suggest that someone perform a specific action, often as friendly advice or encouragement. It can also be used when offering something, such as a drink. On the other hand, 薦める is used to recommend a person or thing as suitable for a particular situation, with a focus on endorsing the subject rather than a specific action.
readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as 勧める , since they mean almost the same thing.

sentences.japanese: この番組を彼に薦められたんだけど、アニメを観るのはあまり好きじゃないんだよね。
sentences.english: He recommended this show to me, but I don’t really like watching anime.

sentences.japanese: コウイチが美味しいと薦めてきたクラブケーキを食べてみたらすごく不味かった。
sentences.english: Koichi said the crab cakes were delicious and recommended them; when I tried them they tasted terrible.

sentences.japanese: ミステリーファンにはこの映画を見ることを薦めます。
sentences.english: I recommend mystery fans go see this movie.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means rot so the verb vocab version is to rot .
readingMnemonic: Remember the word 臭い , which means "stinky"? When something rots, it becomes stinky, and all くさ い .

sentences.japanese: 牛乳は腐りやすいんだから冷蔵庫の外に出しっ放しにしないでね。
sentences.english: Don’t leave milk out of the fridge because it goes bad easily.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means run alongside so the verb vocab version is to run alongside .
readingMnemonic: Imagine yourself on a path designed to run alongside an endless array of so ap ( そ ) bars. As you walk alongside the soap bars, you enjoy their delightful scents. It's a "scent-sational" promenade with soap bars that leaves you feeling squeaky clean!

sentences.japanese: 川の両岸に沿って、ずうっと、美しい桜並木があるんです。
sentences.english: There are beautiful cherry blossom trees all along the river banks.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means shrink so the verb vocab version means to shrink .
readingMnemonic: Jesus couldn't cause the monster to shrink . He had to transform into cheese jesus ( ちぢ ), a more powerful version of himself, in order to shrink the monster down to size.

sentences.japanese: 雷がゴロゴロ鳴っている間、うちの犬は怖がって縮まっていました。
sentences.english: My puppy was shrinking in fear while the thunder was rumbling.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 詰める is "to stuff in" and the kanji 込 is into . When you’re stuffing something into something else, you are going to stuff or to cram it in. Just as in English, this word can also be used in a figurative sense, like cramming knowledge into your head.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji. If you remember your kanji readings, you'll be fine here.

sentences.japanese: なんとか洋服を全部スーツケースに詰め込めました。
sentences.english: I managed to cram all my clothes into my suitcase.

meaningMnemonic: An all loss is when you lose it all. It is a total loss .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 車が全損してしまった場合、修理代は保険で全額支払われないことが多いです。
sentences.english: If it turns out that the car is a total loss, many insurance companies will not pay the full repair cost.

meaningMnemonic: You throw and throw away something. That's why this means to throw away .
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 投げる and 捨てる , combined into one garbage inducing dump of a word.

sentences.japanese: 今朝、六時に目覚ましがなった時に、その時計を投げ捨ててしまいました。
sentences.english: I threw my alarm clock away when it went off at six this morning.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means worship so the verb vocab version is to worship . 拝む generally means to pray to a deity, spirit, or revered object while assuming a worshipping position, such as bowing or clasping one's hands together in prayer. Additionally, 拝む can also mean to see with a sense of respect and reverence.
readingMnemonic: You have to worship the ogre ( おが ), because if you don't it'll eat your face off.

sentences.japanese: 私の家族は、毎朝仏壇の前に集まって仏様に拝みます。
sentences.english: My family gathers in front of our family Buddhist altar to pray to Buddha every morning.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 書く is "to write" and the kanji 込 is into , so this means to write in , to fill out , or to jot down . 書き込む focuses more on the physical action of writing than 書く on its own. This is because 込む stresses that you’re putting words INTO some space, either on paper or on computer.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the word 書く and the kanji 込 combined into one.

sentences.japanese: 急いで申込書に書き込んだ方がいいよ。あと十分で事務所は閉まっちゃうんだから。
sentences.english: You better hurry up and fill out an application. The office will close in ten minutes.

meaningMnemonic: A mistake in letter s is a typo .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: とりあえず今は誤字脱字を見つけてくれればそれでいいから。
sentences.english: For now, all you have to do is find typos.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji!

sentences.japanese: 縦100cm横160cmの窓に合う良いカーテンを探しています。
sentences.english: I’m looking for nice curtains that will suit our 100 centimeter by 160 centimeter window.

meaningMnemonic: Vertical writing is vertical writing . That's when you see Japanese and it's written top to bottom instead of sideways.
readingMnemonic: The readings are the reading you learned with the kanji 縦 and かき (changes to がき ), though the き gets smushed inside the kanji, because it wants to be confusing like that.

sentences.japanese: 文章を縦書にしたいんです。
sentences.english: I want to make the writing vertical.

meaningMnemonic: It's my delight to welcome you, so I give you a big, warm welcome . 歓迎 is a relatively formal word that refers to warmly accepting someone in, like welcoming someone who's arrived somewhere or joined a group.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: カウンターの上に「チップ大歓迎」と書かれた箱がありましたよ。
sentences.english: I saw a box on the counter that had "tips welcome" written on it.

meaningMnemonic: Just imagine a black curtain off in the background. You don't know what's behind it, but you know what's in front of it. Thing is, the thing in front of the curtain is controlled by whoever is behind the black curtain. This person is the wirepuller or mastermind of the situation. Like the Wizard of Oz, or something.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the vocab readings for 黒 and 幕 , though the vocab reading for 幕 is the same as the on'yomi reading, making things easy for you.

sentences.japanese: 結局、あんたが黒幕だったんだな。どうりであの女を殺した時手慣れていたと思ったよ。
sentences.english: So, you are the mastermind, huh? No wonder you seemed so professional when you killed her.
